On the Memorization Behavior of LLMs in Generative Recommendation:
Observations, Implications, and Training Strategies

Sunwoo Kim Affiliation: KAIST Email: kswoo97@kaist.ac.kr    Sunkyung Lee Affiliation: Sungkyunkwan University Email: kijungs@kaist.ac.kr    Clark Mingxuan Ju Affiliation: Snap Inc. Email: sk1027@skku.edu    Donald Loveland Affiliation: Snap Inc. Email: mju@snapchat.com    Bhuvesh Kumar Affiliation: Snap Inc. Email: dloveland@snapchat.com    Kijung Shin Affiliation: KAIST Email: bkumar4@snapchat.com    Neil Shah Affiliation: Snap Inc. Email: nshah@snapchat.com    Liam Collins Affiliation: Snap Inc. Email: lcollins2@snapchat.com
Abstract

Generative recommendation (GR) has emerged as a promising direction for recommender systems. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have been increasingly adopted for GR, as their rich pretrained knowledge is expected to help them generalize beyond common user behavior patterns that traditional memorization-oriented baselines can capture. However, existing LLM-based GR works largely ignore LLMs’ well-known tendency to memorize Satvaty et al. (2024); Li et al. (2025), which, if present in LLMs fine-tuned for GR, would restrict their utilization of pretrained knowledge. In this work, we investigate this concern by examining one-hop memorization, where a model recommends items that are direct successors of items in the training data. We show that LLMs do this more than non-LLM-based GR models–in fact, the vast majority of their gains over GR baselines are actually on users whose target items can be predicted through one-hop memorization. We intuit that improving performance on the remaining users requires LLMs to learn richer item–item relations beyond one-hop transitions. To achieve this, we propose IIRG, a novel training strategy that teaches LLMs to capture: (1) collaborative relations derived from item co-occurrences across multiple hops in user sequences, and (2) semantic relations among items with similar themes, both of which can serve as useful recommendation signals. We show that IIRG significantly improves over LLMs trained solely with standard next-item prediction, with especially large gains for users whose test items are not covered by train-time one-hop transitions.

1 Introduction

Generative recommendation (GR) has recently drawn growing interest within the recommendation community Wang et al. (2025); Ju et al. (2025); Xie et al. (2025). Given a user’s item interaction history, GR methods use a generative model to generate the identifier of the target item, rather than scoring a predefined set of candidate items Senel et al. (2024); Liu et al. (2025b); Hou et al. (2025).

A growing line of work on GR adopts large language models (LLMs) as recommender systems, motivated by their rich pretrained world knowledge Zhou et al. (2025); Xie et al. (2026). These approaches have achieved strong performance on recommendation tasks in both academic Lee et al. (2025); Liu et al. (2025a) and industrial He et al. (2026); D’Amico et al. (2026) settings.

For GR, LLMs are often fine-tuned using next-item prediction because pretrained LLMs are not aware of the specific item set from which they are allowed to recommend, nor do they have sufficient knowledge of user–item interaction patterns. Specifically, given the earlier part of a user’s item interaction sequence, LLMs are fine-tuned to generate the identifier (e.g., semantic- or term-ID) of the next item in the sequence Hong et al. (2025).

While LLMs hold promise for GR through their pretrained knowledge, prior work in NLP suggests a potential obstacle to fulfilling this promise. LLMs are well-known to memorize, i.e. retain certain portions of the training set and later reproduce them at inference time Satvaty et al. (2024); Li et al. (2025). Heavy reliance on such behavior would limit the ability of LLM-based GR models to capitalize on pretrained world knowledge, as their predictions would instead be driven by repetitions of patterns observed in the recommendation training data, just like traditional, non-language informed recommenders. However, this phenomenon remains largely unexplored in LLM-based GR.

To address this issue, we analyze memorization behavior in LLM-based GR. We focus on a widely used LLM-based GR pipeline in which each item is represented by its text features alongside a structured item ID (e.g., semantic ID (SID) or term ID (TID)), which may be trained to align with the LLM’s vocabulary He et al. (2026). The LLM is then fine-tuned to generate the ID of the next item given the user’s previous interaction sequence Lee et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2026). In this setting, we ask two questions: (1) what distinctive memorization behavior do LLMs exhibit compared to non-LLM-based GR models, and (2) how does this behavior relate to recommendation performance?

For the first question, we show that LLMs exhibit strong one-hop memorization. In particular, LLMs memorize one-hop item transitions in the training set—transitions between consecutive items in user sequences—and at inference time base their recommendations on the observed successors of items in the user’s input sequence, as illustrated in Figure 1. This memorization behavior is more pronounced in LLMs than in TIGER, a representative non-LLM-based GR model Rajput et al. (2023), as shown in Figure 2(a). This phenomenon persists after scaling TIGER to a near-LLM size and applying regularization to LLMs, suggesting that model size and overfitting alone are insufficient explanations.

For the second question, we show that the performance gains of LLMs over TIGER largely come from users who benefit from one-hop memorization. Specifically, we divide users into two groups: (1) users whose target item appears in the training set as a next item of any item from their input sequence, and (2) users whose target item does not. We find that LLMs achieve substantially larger improvements over TIGER for the first group, while their performance gains are much smaller for the second group, as shown in Figure 2(b) and (c).

Given that one-hop memorization provides limited information for the target item for users in the second group, we hypothesize that improving performance for these users requires LLMs to learn richer item–item relations beyond one-hop transitions—relations that can connect the user’s input items to the target item. To achieve this goal, we propose IIRG (Item–Item Relation Generation), a simple yet effective training strategy that encourages LLMs to capture such relations.

In a nutshell, given an item, IIRG trains LLMs to generate items that are either collaboratively or semantically relevant to it. For collaborative relations, IIRG uses items that frequently co-occur with the given item across multiple hops in user interaction sequences. For semantic relations, IIRG uses items with semantically relevant textual descriptions, helping the model capture items users may naturally consider together (e.g., related LEGO products or compatible accessories). Our data analysis shows that these relations benefit users outside the coverage of one-hop memorization, reaching a group comparable in size to the users benefiting from one-hop memorization. Note that IIRG is identifier-agnostic, supporting both SIDs and TIDs.

Through experiments, we show that LLMs trained with IIRG consistently improve over an LLM trained solely with next-item prediction, achieving a 21% average gain in Recall@5. The gain is especially pronounced for users whose target items are not covered by one-hop memorization, yielding a 50% gain compared to a 17% gain for users whose target items are covered by such memorization in the Sports dataset (see Figure 2). Our key contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    C1. New finding: We analyze LLMs’ one-hop memorization behavior and its relationship with recommendation performance.

  • •

    C2. New method: We propose IIRG, a training strategy that helps LLMs capture richer item–item relations beyond one-hop memorization.

  • •

    C3. Strong performance: We experimentally validate that IIRG leads to consistent gains over LLM-based recommenders with various ID types, as well as several other baseline methods.

We provide our code and datasets in https://github.com/snap-research/IIRG.

2 Related work

LLM Memorization. LLMs are known to reproduce exact phrases from their pre-training Kassem et al. (2023) and/or fine-tuning data Mireshghallah et al. (2022), though the exact causes remain unclear. Hypothesized explanations involve factors such as model size or duplicated training data Satvaty et al. (2024). In many LLM applications, this reproduction can leak private or copyrighted material Henderson et al. (2023). Several methods have been studied to address this, e.g. data dededuplication Lee et al. (2022b) and specialized decoding Ippolito et al. (2023). However, memorization in LLM-based GR remains underexplored.

Generative recommendation with LLMs. Generative recommendation (GR) methods have been extensively studied Rajput et al. (2023); Li et al. (2024); Xie et al. (2025); Lin et al. (2025). Among these, a promising direction uses pre-trained LLMs to exploit their rich world knowledge Penha et al. (2025). Many approaches use structured item identifiers to mitigate hallucination and facilitate efficient decoding, most notably semantic IDs (SIDs) Kong et al. (2025); He et al. (2026) and term IDs (TIDs) Tan et al. (2024); Lee et al. (2025). After associating each item with such an ID, the LLM is tuned for next-item prediction via autoregressive training on users’ past interaction sequences Zhang et al. (2026); He et al. (2026).

Auxiliary training tasks for LLM-based GR. To improve the GR performance of LLMs, several auxiliary training tasks have been leveraged, often alongside next-item prediction.11 1 Here, auxiliary tasks refer to tasks used for LLM training, rather than those used for ID generation, such as the contrastive learning objective in PLUM He et al. (2026). These tasks can be categorized into three: (1) distillation tasks, which help lightweight LLM-based GR models acquire the reasoning abilities of stronger LLMs Hong et al. (2025); (2) alignment tasks, which help LLMs better understand the identifiers of items Zhang et al. (2026); (3) auxiliary recommendation tasks, such as rating prediction Geng et al. (2022) or item unmasking from user sequences Cao et al. (2024). To our knowledge, none of these tasks explicitly train LLMs to learn item–item relations beyond one-hop transitions in user sequences.

3 Analysis of Memorization in GR

In this section, we first formalize the generative recommendation (GR) setting. Then, we analyze the one-hop memorization behavior of LLMs in comparison with non-LLM-based GR models.

3.1 Problem Formulation

Let 𝒰\mathcal{U} and ℐ\mathcal{I} denote the user and item sets, respectively. Each user u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U} is associated with an item interaction sequence su=(i1(u),i2(u),⋯,i|su|(u))s_{u}=(i^{(u)}_{1},i^{(u)}_{2},\cdots,i^{(u)}_{|s_{u}|}), 22 2 Although |𝒜|\mathcal{|A|} typically denotes the cardinality of a set 𝒜\mathcal{A}, we use |⋅||\cdot| to denote the length of a sequence unless otherwise stated, as our notation primarily concerns sequences. and each item ik∈ℐi_{k}\in\mathcal{I} is represented by its textual metadata t(ik)(i_{k}), such as its title and description, and its identifier id(ik)(i_{k}), such as a semantic ID (SID) He et al. (2026) or term ID (TID) Zhang et al. (2026). Given a user interaction sequence sus_{u}, the goal of GR is to generate the identifier of the item that user uu is most likely to interact with next.

3.2 Analysis setup

Overview. Recall that one-hop memorization refers to a model’s tendency to memorize one-hop item transitions in training data and later recommend the memorized successors of items appearing in the interaction sequence of a test user. To quantify one-hop memorization, we measure the fraction of each model’s top-5 recommendations that correspond to memorized successors of items in the test user’s input sequence. Then, we examine how the performance gains of LLM-based GR models over non-LLM-based GR models are related to one-hop memorization, motivating improvements in LLM-based GR models.

Models and datasets. We consider two GR models: (1) our target model, a Qwen-3.5-4B Yang et al. (2025) LLM trained with a next-item prediction objective under SIDs and TIDs (see Appendix C.3 for further details on each ID type); and (2) TIGER Rajput et al. (2023), a representative non-LLM-based GR baseline. We use three Amazon Reviews datasets He and McAuley (2016), Sports, Toys, and Beauty.

Training. Following Zhang et al. (2026), the LLM is trained for next-item prediction using next-token prediction for a language-formatted item interaction sequence. For the sequence representation, we represent each item iki_{k} in user uu’s interaction sequence sus_{u} by its identifier id(ik)(i_{k}) (either an SID or TID) and title t(ik)(i_{k}). Appendix B.1 provides an example prompt. Based on this input structure, we perform supervised fine-tuning of the LLM. Formally, let 𝒯(su)\mathcal{T}^{(s_{u})} denote the tokenized representation of sequence sus_{u}. Then, the LLM training loss for user uu is:

ℒu=−∑t=T+1|𝒯(su)|log⁡pθ​(𝒯t(su)∣𝒯<t(su),𝒞)|𝒯(su)|−T,\mathcal{L}_{u}=-\sum_{t=T+1}^{\left|\mathcal{T}^{(s_{u})}\right|}\frac{\log p_{\theta}\left(\mathcal{T}^{(s_{u})}_{t}\mid\mathcal{T}^{(s_{u})}_{<t},\mathcal{C}\right)}{|\mathcal{T}^{(s_{u})}|-T}, (1)

where pθp_{\theta} denotes the token-generation probability of the LLM parameterized by θ\theta, 𝒯t(su)\mathcal{T}^{(s_{u})}_{t} is the tt-th token in sequence 𝒯(su)\mathcal{T}^{(s_{u})}, TT is the index of the final token for the anchor item i1(u)i^{(u)}_{1} within sus_{u}, and 𝒞\mathcal{C} denotes the tokens representing the instruction of next-item prediction. We train the baseline, TIGER, following its original paper (Rajput et al., 2023).

Metrics. To quantify a model’s reliance on one-hop memorization, we define the adjacent neighbor set 𝒩⁡(ik)\mathcal{N}(i_{k}) as the multiset of all items that immediately follow iki_{k} in any training user sequence. Next, we define a one-hop-based candidate set for each user. This set is constructed by: (1) aggregating the adjacent neighbors of all items in the user’s sequence (i.e. ℳu=⊎ik∈su𝒩(ik)\mathcal{M}_{u}=\uplus_{i_{k}\in s_{u}}\mathcal{N}(i_{k}) where ⊎\uplus denotes the additive union of multisets) and (2) selecting the min⁡(50,|⋃ik∈su𝒩⁡(ik)|)\min(50,|\bigcup_{i_{k}\in s_{u}}\mathcal{N}(i_{k})|) items with largest multiplicities in ℳu\mathcal{M}_{u} and tie-breaking based on popularity.33 3 We use the top-KK most frequent adjacent neighbors to avoid excessively large candidate sets, which provide limited information for measuring one-hop memorization. Lastly, for each model, we compute the average fraction of its top-55 recommendations that belong to the one-hop-based candidate set.

User groups. We divide users into two groups: the one-hop-memorization-benefiting group and the non-one-hop-memorization-benefiting group. The former consists of users whose one-hop candidate set contains their target item, while the latter consists of the rest. We then measure the recommendation performance of each model on both groups to identify where the performance gains of LLMs primarily come from.

3.3 Results

Reliance on one-hop memorization. As shown in Figure 3(a), LLM-based GR models consistently exhibit a higher one-hop memorization ratio in their top-5 recommendations than TIGER, the non-LLM-based GR baseline. This trend holds for both TIDs and SIDs. This result suggests that LLMs rely more heavily on one-hop memorization than the non-LLM-based GR model. Moreover, this tendency remains even when we (1) apply regularizations to LLMs or (2) scale TIGER to an LLM-comparable size, as detailed in Appendices D.2 and D.3, respectively. This implies that neither model size nor overfitting alone explains the result.

User-wise performance. As shown in Figure 3(b), LLMs achieve larger relative improvements over TIGER for one-hop-memorization-benefiting users than for non-memorization-benefiting users in 5 out of 6 settings. This implies that LLMs’ reliance on one-hop memorization primarily benefits users whose target items are covered by memorized one-hop transitions, but provides limited benefits for the remaining users.

Key implications. Our analysis suggests that relying on one-hop memorization offers limited benefits for users whose target items are not covered by such memorized transitions. We hypothesize that improving performance for these users requires LLMs to learn richer and predictive item–item relations beyond one-hop transitions. These relations can provide additional connections between the user’s input items and the target item. Note that this motivates our training strategy (§ 4).

4 Proposed method: IIRG

To encourage LLMs to learn item–item relations beyond one-hop item transitions, we introduce IIRG (Item–Item Relation Generation), a simple yet effective training strategy that trains an LLM to capture two types of item relationships: (1) collaborative and (2) semantic. Figure 4 provides a visual overview of IIRG. We first motivate and summarize IIRG in § 4.1, then detail its design in § 4.2.

4.1 Overview and intuition for IIRG

Overview. For each item, we construct two sets of “neighbors” to use as item-to-item supervision signals in our auxiliary training tasks. Specifically, for an item iki_{k}, we select (1) collaborative neighbors from items that frequently co-occur with iki_{k} in a multi-hop window within user sequences, and (2) semantic neighbors as items with similar textual descriptions. Then, while training the LLM to predict next items in user sequences, we also train the LLM to generate the corresponding neighbor sets for each item ik∈ℐi_{k}\in\mathcal{I}, enabling it to explicitly learn the relationships between iki_{k} and its neighbors.

Key intuition. Our key objectives in selecting item-to-item supervision signals are whether such relations provide strong predictive information for the target items while remaining distinct from one-hop transitions, as motivated by the implications from our analysis (§ 3.3). We elaborate on how our item-to-item supervision aligns with this goal.

First, for collaborative neighbors, frequently co-purchased items provide strong evidence that interacting with one item increases the likelihood of interacting with the other Sarwar et al. (2001). However, items far apart in a user sequence may reflect different intents and introduce noise. To reduce it, we define collaborative neighbors as items co-occurring within a multi-hop time window.

Second, for semantic neighbors, semantic relevance captures item–item associations useful for recommendation, such as complementarity and/or theme-consistent relations. For instance, if a LEGO enthusiast shows interest in “LEGO City Race Car”, “LEGO City Camper Van” is a high-fidelity semantically-grounded recommendation candidate due to the items’ shared theme.

Evidence from data analysis. To verify whether our collaborative neighbors and semantic neighbors achieve our key objectives, we provide a data analysis in Appendix D.1. In short, we show that (1) these two types of neighbors provide strong predictive signals for users’ target items, comparable to or even stronger than one-hop transitions, and (2) their overlap with one-hop transitions is limited, suggesting that they provide additional, non-redundant signals beyond one-hop transitions.

4.2 Design details of IIRG

Obtaining collaborative neighbors. For collaborative neighbors, we first define an item–item pair weight as the frequency with which they co-appear within a specified time window in user sequences. Specifically, the item-item pair weight wk​qw_{kq} between items iki_{k} and iqi_{q} is defined as follows:

wk​q=∑u∈𝒰𝕀[ik∼W(u)iq],ik∼W(u)iq⇔\displaystyle w_{kq}=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\mathbb{I}[i_{k}\sim^{(u)}_{W}i_{q}],\quad\ i_{k}\sim^{(u)}_{W}i_{q}\iff
∃t,j∈[|su|]:it(u)=ik,ij(u)=iq,0<|t−j|≤W,\displaystyle\exists t,j\in[|s_{u}|]:i^{(u)}_{t}=i_{k},i^{(u)}_{j}=i_{q},0<|t-j|\leq W,

where 𝕀⁡[⋅]\mathbb{I}[\cdot] is the indicator function and WW denotes the time-window length. Lastly, the collaborative neighbor sequence of item iki_{k}, denoted by nkn_{k}, is defined as the sequence of top−N1-N_{1} items sorted in descending order of their pairwise weights wk​qw_{kq} among all iq∈ℐ∖{ik}i_{q}\in\mathcal{I}\setminus\{i_{k}\}. We also consider excluding one-hop transitions when obtaining collaborative neighbors, but this variant underperforms our approach; additional discussion is in Appendix D.4.

Obtaining semantic neighbors. For semantic neighbors, we first encode each item’s textual description into an embedding. Specifically, for each item ik∈ℐi_{k}\in\mathcal{I}, we use a pre-trained language embedding model ff to obtain its embedding 𝐳k=f⁡(t​(ik))\mathbf{z}_{k}=f(\texttt{t}(i_{k})), where t​(ik)\texttt{t}(i_{k}) is a textual description of iki_{k}. Lastly, the semantic neighbor sequence of item iki_{k}, denoted by mkm_{k}, is defined as the sequence of top−N2-N_{2} items sorted in descending order of their cosine similarities (i.e., (𝐳kT​𝐳q)/(‖𝐳𝐤‖​‖𝐳𝐪‖)(\mathbf{z}^{T}_{k}\mathbf{z}_{q})/(\|\mathbf{z_{k}}\|\|\mathbf{z_{q}}\|)) for each item ik∈ℐi_{k}\in\mathcal{I} among all iq∈ℐ∖{ik}i_{q}\in\mathcal{I}\setminus\{i_{k}\}. Alternatively, instead of performing embedding-based full search over all items, we can efficiently retrieve semantic neighbors using semantic-ID-based hashing, while still achieving competitive performance; additional details are in Appendix D.6.

Training objective. After obtaining collaborative neighbors nkn_{k} and semantic neighbors mkm_{k} for each item ik∈ℐi_{k}\in\mathcal{I}, we train an LLM to capture these relations by learning to generate the corresponding neighbors for a given iki_{k}. To this end, as in next-item prediction (§ 3.2), each item ik∈ℐi_{k}\in\mathcal{I} is represented by its ID id(ik)(i_{k}) (either an SID or TID) and title t(ik)(i_{k}). We then construct input prompts for the collaborative-neighbor and semantic-neighbor generation tasks; examples of these prompts are provided in Appendices B.2 and B.3, respectively.

Lastly, we perform supervised fine-tuning of the LLM. Formally, let 𝒯(nk)\mathcal{T}^{(n_{k})} and 𝒯(mk)\mathcal{T}^{(m_{k})} denote the tokenized representations of the sequences nkn_{k} and mkm_{k}, respectively. Similarly, let 𝒯(ik)\mathcal{T}^{(i_{k})} denote the tokenized representation of input item iki_{k}. Then, the LLM training loss for item iki_{k}’s (1) collaborative neighbor generation ℒk(C)\mathcal{L}^{(C)}_{k} and (2) semantic neighbor generation ℒk(S)\mathcal{L}^{(S)}_{k} is defined as follows:

ℒk(C)=∑t=1|𝒯(nk)|log⁡pθ​(𝒯t(nk)∣𝒯<t(nk),𝒫)−|𝒯(nk)|,\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{(C)}_{k}=\sum_{t=1}^{\left|\mathcal{T}^{(n_{k})}\right|}\frac{\log p_{\theta}\left(\mathcal{T}^{(n_{k})}_{t}\mid\mathcal{T}^{(n_{k})}_{<t},\mathcal{P}\right)}{-{|\mathcal{T}^{(n_{k})}|}}, (2)
ℒk(S)=∑t=1|𝒯(mk)|log⁡pθ​(𝒯t(mk)∣𝒯<t(mk),𝒮)−|𝒯(mk)|,\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{(S)}_{k}=\sum_{t=1}^{\left|\mathcal{T}^{(m_{k})}\right|}\frac{\log p_{\theta}\left({\mathcal{T}^{(m_{k})}_{t}\mid\mathcal{T}^{(m_{k})}_{<t},\mathcal{S}}\right)}{-{|\mathcal{T}^{(m_{k})}|}}, (3)

where pθp_{\theta} denotes the token-generation probability of the LLM parameterized by θ\theta, 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t} is the t−t-th token of the sequence 𝒯\mathcal{T} with 𝒯0=∅\mathcal{T}_{0}=\emptyset, and 𝒫\mathcal{P} and 𝒮\mathcal{S} denote the token representations of the instructions for collaborative neighbor generation and semantic neighbor generation, respectively.

All together: IIRG. Overall, IIRG jointly trains an LLM on three tasks: (1) next-item prediction, optimized with ℒu\mathcal{L}_{u} (Eq. (1)); (2) collaborative-neighbor generation; and (3) semantic-neighbor generation.44 4 One alternative is to use the neighbor generation tasks for continued pre-training, but this approach underperforms IIRG. We provide further discussions in Appendix D.5. Each training batch contains a mixture of samples from the three tasks. Formally, let 𝒰(b)⊆𝒰\mathcal{U}_{(b)}\subseteq\mathcal{U} denote the users in batch bb for next-item prediction, and let ℐ(b)(C)⊆ℐ\mathcal{I}^{(C)}_{(b)}\subseteq\mathcal{I}, and ℐ(b)(S)⊆ℐ\mathcal{I}^{(S)}_{(b)}\subseteq\mathcal{I} denote the items in batch bb for which collaborative neighbors and semantic neighbors are generated, respectively. Then, for batch bb, IIRG updates the parameters of the LLM via gradient descent by minimizing:

ℒ=∑u∈𝒰(b)ℒuB+∑ik∈ℐ(b)(C)λ1​ℒk(C)B+∑it∈ℐ(b)(S)λ2​ℒt(S)B,\mathcal{L}=\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}_{(b)}}\frac{\mathcal{L}_{u}}{B}+\sum_{i_{k}\in\mathcal{I}^{(C)}_{(b)}}\frac{\lambda_{1}\mathcal{L}^{(C)}_{k}}{B}+\sum_{i_{t}\in\mathcal{I}^{(S)}_{(b)}}\frac{\lambda_{2}\mathcal{L}^{(S)}_{t}}{B},

where BB denotes the batch size, and λ1\lambda_{1} and λ2\lambda_{2} denote the hyperparameters that control the effects of the collaborative- and semantic-neighbor generation losses, respectively.

5 Experiments

In this section, we evaluate the effectiveness of IIRG in the recommendation tasks.

5.1 Experimental setting

Datasets. For experiments, we use three benchmark sequential recommendation domains from the Amazon Review dataset He and McAuley (2016): Sports, Toys, and Beauty. We report additional results on the Yelp dataset in Appendix D.10.

Evaluation. Following common practice in sequential recommendation Kang and McAuley (2018); Geng et al. (2022), we use the leave-one-out protocol. Specifically, for each user sequence, we use the last item for testing, the second-to-last item for validation, and the remaining interactions for training. We consider the full-item ranking setting, where all items are considered as possible recommendation candidates. For metrics, we use Recall@KK and NDCG@KK, where K∈{5,10}K\in\{5,10\}.

Baseline methods. We compare against 17 baselines from four categories. Specifically, we use (1) five traditional models (LightGCN He et al. (2020), SimGCL Yu et al. (2022), SASRec Kang and McAuley (2018), FDSA Zhang et al. (2019), S3-Rec Zhou et al. (2020)), (2) two non-LLM-based GR models (TIGER Rajput et al. (2023), LETTER Wang et al. (2024)), (3) four GR methods that use joint training of auxiliary tasks and next-item prediction (P5 Geng et al. (2022), ReAT Cao et al. (2024), LC-Rec Zheng et al. (2024a), EAGER-LLM Hong et al. (2025)), and (4) six LLM-based GR models using SIDs (PLUM He et al. (2026), OneRec-Think Liu et al. (2025b)) or TIDs (Naive (LLM trained solely with next-item prediction), GRAM Lee et al. (2025), GRLM Zhang et al. (2026), AgenticTagger Xie et al. (2026)). Further baseline details are in Appendix C.5.

Proposed method: IIRG. We fully fine-tune the backbone LLM as described in § 4.2. We use TIDs as the default item IDs, except when evaluating the effectiveness of IIRG under SIDs in § 5.3. Note that each user’s target item is explicitly excluded from the user sequence when obtaining collaborative neighbors to prevent data leakage. Item ID details and IIRG details are provided in Appendices C.3 and C.4, respectively.

5.2 Recommendation performance

Setup. For non-LLM baselines, we use the backbone models from their original papers. For LLM-based baselines, we use Qwen-3.5-4B Yang et al. (2025), the same backbone as IIRG, and fully fine-tune it. We use the item identifiers proposed in each paper, except for LLM-based GR models with auxiliary training, where we use the same identifiers as IIRG for a fair comparison of training strategies. When our reproduced results are lower than the originally reported results, we use the results reported in the corresponding paper, as their methods were also evaluated under the same setting. In addition, we further analyze cold-start item recommendation in Appendix D.9.

Result. As shown in Table 1, IIRG consistently performs best across all datasets and metrics. Two points stand out. First, IIRG consistently improves over the LLM trained solely with next-item prediction (Naive), achieving a 21% average improvement in Recall@5 across datasets. Second, IIRG outperforms all baseline training methods in all the datasets, demonstrating that it is a more effective training method than existing training baselines.

5.3 Generalization across item IDs

Setup. We showed the effectiveness of IIRG under TIDs in § 5.2. To examine whether this improvement generalizes to SIDs, we repeat the experiments from § 5.2 using SIDs as item IDs. For a fair comparison, Naive, LC-Rec, and IIRG all use the SIDs from He et al. (2026); we use LC-Rec as the strongest baseline among those to which SIDs are applicable.55 5 Naive with SIDs corresponds to PLUM He et al. (2026). Additional results with different SIDs are provided in Appendix D.11.

Result. As shown in Figure 5, IIRG consistently improves over Naive and outperforms LC-Rec, the strongest applicable SID baseline, across the datasets. This result indicates that the effectiveness of IIRG still holds under semantic IDs.

5.4 Design goal achievement

Setup. We examine whether IIRG reduces the reliance on one-hop memorization exhibited by an LLM trained solely with next-item prediction, and whether it achieves stronger performance gains for users who do not benefit from one-hop memorization. To this end, we repeat the analysis in § 3 for IIRG and compare its results against Naive.

Result. As shown in Figure 6(a), IIRG reduces Naive’s reliance on one-hop memorization. Also, as shown in Figure 6(b), IIRG yields an average gain over Naive of 40% for users who do not benefit from one-hop memorization, versus 16% for users who do, across datasets and IDs. This suggests that IIRG provides strong gains for non-memorization-benefiting users, aligning with our key objective.

5.5 Ablation study

Setup. We analyze whether all key components of IIRG are necessary for achieving strong performance. We remove collaborative neighbor generation, semantic neighbor generation, or both. TIDs are used as item IDs. In Appendix D.8, we further study (1) a variant trained on random neighbors and (2) heuristics that directly use collaborative or semantic neighbors as recommendations, both of which underperform IIRG.

Result. As shown in Table 2, IIRG consistently improves its variants across the datasets, demonstrating that both neighbor generation tasks are necessary for achieving strong performance.

6 Conclusion

In this work, we investigate memorization behavior in LLM-based GR. We first show that LLMs rely more heavily on one-hop memorization than non-LLM-based GR models, and that their performance gains over these models are largely concentrated among users who benefit from such memorization. Motivated by this, we propose IIRG, a simple yet effective training strategy that helps LLMs capture richer item–item relations beyond one-hop transitions. Through experiments, we show that IIRG consistently improves over LLMs trained solely with next-item prediction, especially for users who do not benefit from one-hop memorization.

Limitations

Unknown underlying factor. While we uncover one-hop memorization in LLMs and analyze its impact on recommendation performance, we do not identify the underlying factors that explain why this one-hop memorization emerges. More broadly, prior work in the general NLP literature has proposed several possible explanations for LLM memorization Satvaty et al. (2024), although the dominant factor remains unclear. Notably, one key hypothesis from NLP, model size, does not appear to explain our observations in GR, as discussed in Appendix D.3. Identifying the primary factors behind one-hop memorization in LLM-based GR is therefore an important direction for future work.

Limited LLM types. In this work, we use the Qwen-3.5 family Yang et al. (2025) across diverse model sizes. However, several other LLM families exist, such as Llama Grattafiori et al. (2024) and Mistral Jiang et al. (2024). Exploring whether similar one-hop memorization behavior appears across other LLM families would be an interesting direction for assessing the generality of our findings.

Ethical Considerations

This work relies solely on publicly available datasets, publicly released models, and open-source code. We do not collect new user data, use proprietary interaction logs, or conduct any human-subject data collection or annotation. Therefore, we believe that our experiments do not introduce additional privacy risks beyond those already associated with the public resources used in this study.

Appendix A Details of item identifiers

Item identifiers are structured discrete representations of items that enable LLMs to memorize item-specific information and generate item recommendations. Largely, item identifiers are categorized into: (1) semantic identifiers (semantic IDs) and (2) term-based identifiers (term IDs).

A.1 Semantic identifiers

Semantic identifiers (semantic IDs) are discrete code sequences that represent individual items. For example, an item iki_{k} can be represented by a semantic ID sequence (6,102,47)(6,102,47). Such semantic IDs are often generated from item metadata using discrete representation learning techniques, such as RQ-VAE Lee et al. (2022a) and Residual K-Means Zhou et al. (2025). Despite each semantic ID having an encoded meaning that captures item metadata information, LLMs do not have prior knowledge of these identifiers. Therefore, instead of directly representing each item with integer sequences, methods typically do vocabulary expansion with special tokens for each unique integer at each position to represent the corresponding code, following prior studies Zheng et al. (2024a); He et al. (2026). For example, the semantic ID (6,102,47)(6,102,47) can be represented as a sequence of three position-specific special tokens, [<a6><b102><c47>][<{a_{6}}><{b_{102}}><{c_{47}}>], where <a6><{a_{6}}> corresponds to the index-6 code at the first position, <b102><{b_{102}}> corresponds to the index-102 code at the second position, and <c47><{c_{47}}> corresponds to the index-47 code at the last position. Often, these special tokens are aligned with the LLM’s token space through a dedicated training procedure, such as generating the codes from a given item title He et al. (2026).

A.2 Term-based identifiers

One key challenge in using term-based identifiers for LLM-based generative retrieval is aligning the special tokens corresponding to the codes with the LLM’s token space, so that the LLM can effectively understand and use these codes Zhang et al. (2026). To avoid this cost, a promising research direction is to use terms (i.e., keywords that represent the characteristics of each item) to represent each item Tan et al. (2024). For example, an item with title "Retrospec Bicycles Urban/Fixed Gear Saddle" can be represented as ["Cycling", "Bicycle-part", "Saddle", "Fixed-gear"]. In this way, existing language tokens can be naturally used to represent items, allowing LLMs to interpret them without additional alignment steps.

Appendix C Experimental details

In this section, we present further experimental details of our work.

C.1 Dataset statistics

Table 3 presents the statistics of the datasets used in this work, including number of users, items, and user-item interactions.

C.2 Machines

Our work is conducted on Google Cloud Platform. Each training job is run on a single GCP a2-highgpu-8g VM node equipped with 96 vCPUs, 680 GB of memory, and 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, each with 40 GB of GPU memory. However, for training and evaluation of Qwen-3.5-9B backbone LLM, we use a single GCP a2-ultragpu-8g VM node equipped with 96 vCPUs, 1,360 GB of memory, and 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, each with 80 GB of GPU memory. The code implementation is largely inspired by Zhang et al. (2026), and the detailed LLM fine-tuning protocol is based on LLaMA-Factory (Zheng et al., 2024b).

C.3 Item identifiers of IIRG

As discussed in Section 5, IIRG can be coupled with both term IDs and semantic IDs. We now elaborate on how we obtain the respective identifiers used as item identifiers.

Term IDs (TIDs). We construct four keywords for each item, where each keyword captures a different level of the item’s hierarchical characteristics. Specifically, the first keyword represents the most general attribute, shared by many items in the item space, while the last keyword represents the most specific attribute, shared by only a few items. To obtain these keywords, we first retrieve the 500 nearest neighbors of each item by sorting other items according to the cosine similarity between their textual-description representations and that of the target item. Then, we build the following four item groups:

  • •

    Group 1. Three items randomly sampled from ranks 51 to 500.

  • •

    Group 2. Three items randomly sampled from ranks 11 to 50.

  • •

    Group 3. Three items randomly sampled from ranks 5 to 10.

  • •

    Group 4. A single most similar item.

Then, we prompt the LLM to generate the characteristics shared between the target item and the items in each group. The characteristic identified for Group 1 is used as the first keyword, while the characteristic identified for Group 4 is used as the last keyword.

After generating the four keywords for each item, we refine them by merging semantically equivalent keywords expressed in different forms, such as singular/plural variants and synonyms. This standardization improves consistency across items, making it easier for the LLM-based generative recommender to memorize and generate item representations. To this end, for each keyword level, we aggregate the generated keywords and use an LLM to construct a mapping function that maps semantically equivalent terms to a unified keyword. For scalability, we process keywords in batches rather than feeding all terms to the LLM at once, where each batch contains a subset of the total keywords. We repeat this re-mapping process until convergence, defined as fewer than 10 keywords being changed between iterations.

Semantic IDs (SIDs). For semantic item identifiers, we adopt the identifiers proposed by He et al. (2026). Specifically, we apply RQ-VAE-based vector quantization Lee et al. (2022a) together with co-purchase-based contrastive learning across items. We fix the three-level codebook sizes to (1024,512,256)(1024,512,256), and set the training epochs, learning rate, weight decay, and contrastive-learning loss weight to 150150, 10−310^{-3}, 10−610^{-6}, and 10−110^{-1}, respectively.

After obtaining the semantic identifier for each item, we perform continued pre-training to align the newly added special tokens corresponding to semantic identifier codes after vocabulary expansion. To this end, we freeze the LLM-based generative recommender and its existing language-token embeddings, updating only the special tokens corresponding to the semantic identifier codes. Each training sample is item-level: the input is the item title, and the output is the semantic identifier sequence of the corresponding item. This step is performed for 5 epochs with a learning rate of 10−310^{-3}.

C.4 Details for IIRG

Backbone models and implementation. For the pretrained language embedding model, we use the Qwen-3-8B embedding model Zhang et al. (2025). To build term identifiers, we use the instruction-tuned Qwen-3.5-9B model Yang et al. (2025) for draft keyword generation and keyword refinement. To build semantic identifiers, we use two-layer MLPs as encoders and decoders, with a hidden dimension of 256256. All models are trained with the AdamW optimizer Loshchilov and Hutter (2019), and LLM fine-tuning is implemented based on deepspeed Rasley et al. (2020). For efficiency, model training is performed using bfloat16 precision, except for the 9B models, where we use float32 precision because bfloat16 led to numerical instability and NaN values.

Hyperparameters. We train IIRG for 3 epochs with a fixed batch size of 128. Gradient accumulation is used because processing all 128 data points in a single update is not feasible on 40GB GPUs. The co-purchased neighbor generation loss weight λ1\lambda_{1} is fixed to 11, and the number of semantic neighbors N2N_{2} is fixed to 55. We fix the window size in co-purchase neighbor generation WW to 55. We tune the following hyperparameters: the learning rate γ\gamma in {5×10−5,10−4}\{5\times 10^{-5},10^{-4}\}, the weight decay ω\omega in {0,10−2}\{0,10^{-2}\}, the semantic neighbor generation loss weights λ2\lambda_{2} in {10−1,1}\{10^{-1},1\}, and the numbers of collaborative neighbors N1N_{1} in {5,7}\{5,7\}.

Inference of IIRG. For final inference, we use the typical beam-search used in language models Sutskever et al. (2014). Specifically, for each user, the LLM autoregressively generates 20 beams with a fixed number of tokens, and each beam is mapped to an item based on its identifier and the generated output. For the final matching, we follow the matching strategy proposed by Zhang et al. (2026). Note that more than 99.9% of beams are accurately matched to the existing item, which we elaborate in Appendix D.7. When an output beam corresponds to collided items (i.e., items sharing the same identifier), we select the most popular item as the final recommendation for that beam.

C.5 Baseline details

We elaborate on the details regarding the baseline methods used in this work.

Traditional recommender systems. All models are trained with the AdamW Loshchilov and Hutter (2019) optimizer. The backbone architectures of these methods follow those used in the original works. We set the hidden dimension size and weight decay of all baseline methods to 128 and 10−610^{-6}, respectively. We train each model for 200 epochs, and select the model checkpoint with the best validation Recall@10 results. The learning rates of these models are tuned in {10−3,5×10−4,10−4}\{10^{-3},5\times 10^{-4},10^{-4}\}.

Non-LLM-based GR models. All models are trained with the AdamW Loshchilov and Hutter (2019) optimizer. For non-LLM-based GR models, we use the Transformer encoder-decoder architecture Vaswani et al. (2017) as the backbone generative retrieval model. We set the hidden dimension size and weight decay of all baseline methods to 256 and 10−610^{-6}, respectively. We train each model for 100 epochs, and select the model checkpoint with the best validation Recall@10 results. We set the generation output beam-size as 2020, and tune the learning rate in {10−3,5×10−4,10−4}\{10^{-3},5\times 10^{-4},10^{-4}\}.

LLM-based GR models. All models are trained with the AdamW Loshchilov and Hutter (2019) optimizer. For LLM-based GR models that use specialized identifiers and provide official implementations (i.e., GRAM Lee et al. (2025) and GRLM Zhang et al. (2026)), we use their implementations for term identifier generation. For methods without official implementations (i.e., AgenticTagger Xie et al. (2026) and PLUM He et al. (2026)), we implement the identifier generation step following the details provided in their manuscripts. For methods that require a teacher LLM (i.e., P5 Geng et al. (2022), LC-Rec Zheng et al. (2024a), and EAGER-LLM Hong et al. (2025)), where the LLM-based GR model learns from the teacher’s reasoning process, we use Gemini-2.5-Flash Comanici et al. (2025) as the teacher LLM via API access. The overall training pipeline and hyperparameter configuration are kept the same as those of IIRG, except that we tune the learning rate for each method in {10−4,5×10−5}\{10^{-4},5\times 10^{-5}\}. All LLM-based GR methods use the same inference strategy as in IIRG.

Appendix D Additional experimental results

In this section, we provide additional experimental results omitted from the main manuscript due to the space constraint.

D.1 Informativeness of proposed neighbors

Recall that in Section 4, we introduce two types of neighbors that we use as our training objectives: collaborative neighbors and semantic neighbors. In this section, we analyze the informativeness of such neighbors, whether such neighbors can provide effective signal for recommending items to users who do not benefit from the one-hop memorization. To this end, we conduct three analyses: (RQ1) to what extent the neighbors of items in a user’s interaction sequence contain the target item, (RQ2) to what extent these neighbors benefit users who are not sufficiently benefited by one-hop memorization, and (RQ3) whether these neighbors provide signals distinct from one-hop memorization.

Setup. We consider three heuristic candidate sets:

  • •

    Memorization-based: Each user’s candidates are the one-hop memorized items derived from the user’s input sequence, following Section 3.2.

  • •

    Collaborative-neighbor-based: Each user’s candidates are the top-15 most frequent collaborative neighbors of each item in the user’s input sequence.

  • •

    Semantic-neighbor-based: Each user’s candidates are the top-15 items with the most similar textual-description embeddings to each item in the user’s input sequence.

Then, min⁡(50,|⋃ik∈su𝒩⁡(ik)|)\min(50,|\bigcup_{i_{k}\in s_{u}}\mathcal{N}(i_{k})|) candidates are selected for each user uu as in Section 3.2. Lastly, to answer these research questions, we measure: (A1) the number of users whose target item is included in each candidate set, (A2) the number of users who benefit from the two neighbor types but not from one-hop memorization, and (A3) the average Jaccard similarity between different candidate sets for each user.

Result. Results are provided in Figure 13. As shown in (a), our collaborative and semantic neighbors cover a fraction of users comparable to one-hop memorization. In addition, as shown in (b), their pairwise Jaccard similarity with one-hop neighbors remains below 0.5, indicating that these neighbor types provide non-redundant information. Lastly, as shown in (c), among non-memorization-benefiting users, our neighbors cover a group comparable in size to the memorization-benefiting group, suggesting that our supervision signals provide predictive information comparable to or even stronger than one-hop memorization.

D.2 Effect of regularization techniques

In this section, we explore whether common regularization techniques can alleviate the LLM’s tendency to rely on the transition patterns (Section 3).

Setup. We use four regularization techniques in our analysis: (1) LoRA Hu et al. (2022); (2) model-size reduction, using a 0.8B-parameter LLM while all other LLMs in our analysis use 4B-parameter models; (3) L2L_{2} weight decay in the optimizer; and (4) early stopping at epoch 2 instead of the original 3 epochs. We use term IDs as item identifiers. We compare the methods by fine-tuning the LLM for the next-item prediction task with each regularization technique. We use the Beauty dataset.

Result 1: Failure of LoRA. We find that LoRA fails to generate valid recommendation outputs in our setting. Specifically, 94% of the outputs generated by the LoRA-fine-tuned LLM are invalid. These invalid outputs either consist of natural-language reasoning that does not explicitly mention an item (e.g., “Given the user interaction history, the user is likely to purchase camping products”), or contain item identifiers that do not exist in the item space. This trend holds across different LoRA ranks: r=16r=16, corresponding to 1% of the total parameters, r=64r=64, corresponding to 7% of the total parameters, and r=256r=256, corresponding to 13% of the total parameters. This suggests that training a sufficient number of LLM parameters is necessary for enabling the LLM to both follow the desired output format and memorize valid item identifiers.

Result 2: Other methods. As shown in Figure 14, all three regularization techniques fail to reduce one-hop memorization without hurting recommendation performance. In contrast, IIRG reduces memorization behavior while improving downstream task performance, achieving the largest gains in both aspects. This suggests that IIRG addresses the memorization behavior more effectively than common regularization techniques.

D.3 Effect of model size

In this section, we explore whether the one-hop memorization behavior of LLMs has significant correlation with the size of the GR model.

Setup. We evaluate four LLMs of different sizes: 0.8B, 2B, 4B, and 9B parameters. All models are from the same family: Qwen-3.5 Yang et al. (2025). We also scale TIGER, a non-LLM-based GR model, to a near-LLM size of 1.4B parameters, which is roughly 470×\times larger than the 3M-parameter TIGER model used throughout our work. We use the term IDs as item identifiers and measure the reliance of each method on one-hop memorization as in § 3.

Result. As shown in Figure 15, model size does not show a clear trend with the one-hop memorization ratio. This suggests that model size alone does not clearly explain reliance on one-hop memorization.

D.4 Discussions on excluding one-hop transitions from collaborative neighbors

Note that when constructing collaborative neighbors (§ 4.2), we treat all items appearing within a window of size WW around each item as its collaborative neighbor candidates. This often includes the one-hop successor as well, which may preserve the model’s reliance on one-hop memorization. We further analyze whether removing such successors leads to performance improvements.

Setup. An alternative design is to exclude the one-hop successor of the corresponding item and use only the remaining 2​W−12W-1 items as co-purchase neighbors, which more explicitly reduces reliance on one-hop memorization. We then apply the same selection strategy as in § 4.2 to select N1N_{1} items, and use the resulting neighbors as supervision signals for the collaborative neighbor generation task. We use TIDs as item identifiers.

Result. As shown in Table 5, our current design outperforms the alternative that explicitly removes one-hop transition items. We hypothesize that this removal may bias the LLM too strongly toward multi-hop relations, causing it to underutilize one-hop relations that still provide useful predictive signals for certain user groups. Therefore, the current design of IIRG may better balance one-hop and multi-hop relations, which are both important for strong performance.

D.5 Discussions on joint training

Our preliminary analysis shows that joint learning outperforms continued pre-training, where the LLM is first trained on our two neighbor generation tasks and then further fine-tuned for next-item prediction. We hypothesize that this is because, in the latter approach, the LLM tends to forget the rich item relations learned through our tasks and instead reverts to focusing on local transition patterns learned from the next-item prediction task, consistent with observations in LLM continued fine-tuning literature Luo et al. (2025).

D.6 Efficient semantic neighbor generation

Search strategy. Note that semantic neighbors are obtained from item embeddings encoded from item textual descriptions (Section 4.2). A full search over all item embeddings incurs quadratic cost with respect to the number of items. To reduce this, we introduce an efficient search strategy based on each item’s semantic identifier. Instead of performing dense search over all item embeddings, we select the top-KK items according to the number of semantic identifier codes they share with the target item. Ties are broken by prioritizing more popular items.

Setup. We compare the performance of the two retrieval strategies, as well as the performance without our training strategy. In all cases, we use semantic identifiers as item identifiers. We use the Toys dataset for training and evaluation.

Result. As shown in Figure 16, even when semantic neighbors are retrieved using semantic IDs (SIDs) rather than dense embeddings, the resulting model achieves clear gains over the Naive LLM trained only with next-item prediction. Moreover, the gap from full dense embedding search (Emb) remains small, suggesting that SID-based retrieval offers an efficient alternative strategy with limited performance loss.

D.7 Output validity analysis

One undesirable behavior in generative recommendation is generating non-existent items. We therefore verify whether IIRG improves valid item generation for both semantic-ID and term-ID settings.

Setup. Recall that we generate 2020 beams for each user. Across all beams for all users, we compute the ratio of generated beams that are successfully decoded and mapped to the item space.

Result. As shown in Table 6, around 99% of the outputs generated by IIRG can be mapped to actual items, demonstrating that IIRG rarely produces hallucinated item identifiers.

D.8 Additional ablation studies

We conduct two ablation studies to analyze the design choices of IIRG. Specifically, we consider: (1) an LLM trained with randomly sampled neighbors instead of the collaborative and semantic neighbors introduced in § 4; and (2) heuristic methods that directly use collaborative or semantic neighbors as recommendation outputs.

Setup 1. We consider a variant that randomly samples collaborative and semantic neighbors instead of the strategies described in § 4.2, which we call Random. We also compare whether this variant harms the performance of Naive, which is trained solely on next-item prediction. We use TIDs as item IDs.

Result 1. As shown in Table 7, (1) IIRG significantly outperforms Random, and (2) Random even degrades the performance of Naive. This suggests that, for IIRG to achieve strong performance, its supervision signal should be predictive of users’ test items.

Setup 2. We consider four heuristics: (V1) For each item in the user’s input sequence, we sample the top five most frequently co-purchased items, aggregate the candidates, and select 10 final recommendations based on their multiplicity, with popularity-based tie-breaking. (V2) Overall structure is the same as V1, but we only aggregate candidates of the last-2 interacted items of the user. (V3) For each item in the user’s input sequence, we sample the top five items with highest textual representation similarity, aggregate the candidates, and select 10 final recommendations based on their multiplicity. (V4) Overall structure is the same as V3, but we only aggregate candidates of the last-2 interacted items of the user.

Result 2. As shown in Table 8, IIRG outperforms all variants, demonstrating that training LLMs to capture neighbor relations for recommendation is more effective than simply using our collaborative and semantic relations directly.

D.9 Cold-start-item recommendation

We examine how the performance improvement of IIRG over Naive, an LLM trained solely with next-item prediction, varies between cold-start and warm-start target items.

Setup. We divide users into two groups based on the interaction frequency of their target item: (1) cold-item users, whose target item has at most 88 interactions, and (2) warm-item users, whose target item has more than 88 interactions. We then compare the performance improvement within each user group.

Result. As shown in Figure 17, the percentage improvement of IIRG over Naive is larger for cold-item users than for warm-item users, suggesting that IIRG is especially effective at recommending cold-start items. We hypothesize that this is because IIRG’s neighbor generation tasks, particularly semantic neighbor generation, provide additional supervision for cold-start items, leading to larger performance gains.

D.10 Performance on the Yelp dataset

We evaluate the effectiveness of IIRG beyond Amazon Review datasets.

Setup. We use Yelp, a restaurant review dataset.66 6 https://www.yelp.com/dataset We employ the same training and evaluation setting as in § 5.2, and use TIDs as item identifiers. We examine whether IIRG can improve over Naive, an LLM trained solely with next-item prediction, on the Yelp dataset.

Result. As shown in Table 9, IIRG improves the performance of Naive on the Yelp dataset as well, demonstrating that its effectiveness is not limited to Amazon review datasets.

D.11 Generalization to other semantic IDs

As detailed in Section 5 and Appendix C.3, our main analysis and experiments use PLUM He et al. (2026) SIDs. We further examine whether our findings generalize to other types of SIDs.

Setup. We use Residual K-Means (R-K-Means) SIDs Zhou et al. (2025) as item identifiers. We then analyze the memorization reliance and recommendation performance of Naive, an LLM trained solely with next-item prediction, and IIRG, both using R-K-Means SIDs.

Result. As shown in Figure 18, Naive relies more heavily on memorization than TIGER, a non-LLM-based GR model. Moreover, IIRG reduces Naive’s memorization behavior and improves its recommendation performance across all datasets. These results suggest that our observations and the effectiveness of IIRG are not restricted to a particular SID design.
